title: The Body Unveiled
summary: 201 sculptures trace the nude figure from fragmentary studies and covered poses to intimacy and explicit sexual imagery.
invitation: The exhibition starts with partial views and studies, then progresses through full nudity, more exposed poses, intimate groups, and explicit scenes. Works of similar visual explicitness are ordered by date.
viewingNote: This exhibition includes full nudity and explicit sexual imagery.

works.text: SMK records this Farnese Dionysus as a plaster cast of an ancient torso. The cast’s maker and production date are unrecorded. Identifying a torso as Dionysus depends partly on comparison with surviving classical types, making the modern name an argument as well as a label. The upper body twists above the surviving seated thighs. The broken edges put the angle between ribcage and hips on display without requiring a reconstruction of the missing limbs.

This scan records a plaster in Denmark’s Royal Cast Collection after the Crouching Venus type, which the catalog dates to the third century BCE. A compact crouch compresses the many-view sculpture into a shape that can unfold as a viewer walks around it. The squat brings knee, elbow, and chest into a tight arrangement. Follow the turning head and raised hand to see how the pose opens above the folded legs.

SMK acquired this plaster of Denys Puech’s Muse in 1900, after the 1888 marble composition. The kneeling figure mourns André Chénier, the poet executed during the French Revolution. Taking a poet’s muse out of the monument and into a cast collection changes the figure from part of a commemoration into a recorded sculptural type. The long hair gathers the poet’s head into the curve of the muse’s embrace. Bent hips, folded knees and drapery concentrate the grief in a close, low arrangement.

SMK acquired this plaster relief in 1898. It reproduces Apollo from the east frieze of the Pergamon Altar, whose ancient prototype dates to about 170–155 BCE. The Pergamon association identifies the cast’s reference point without requiring a reconstruction of what the absent parts looked like. The chest thrusts out from the slab as drapery sweeps down beside it. An angled view shows how much of the turn the sculptor created in the shallow space between body and background.

This nineteenth-century acquisition is a plaster after a marble from Capua that SMK identifies as a Roman copy of a Hellenistic sculpture. The subject may be Psyche or Aphrodite. The identification of the torso with Psyche is an act of comparison with other works, since the surviving fragment offers limited attributes. The head tips down while the chest turns gently forward. Drapery low on the body creates a rising diagonal that continues the turn even where the arms are missing.

Solsona documented her Mediterrània composition in 2009 with a life-size bronze at Banyuls-sur-Mer. The scan publisher locates this example in Carcassonne, and its relationship to the Banyuls cast is unconfirmed. Recording one version separately from the composition matters when an outdoor figure survives through examples with different casting histories. The raised knee lifts the seated silhouette while both hands press into the base. That spread of supports makes the pose feel stable even as the body opens upward.

SMK’s cast follows a second-century Roman marble unearthed at Hadrian’s Villa in 1881. The plaster entered the collection from the Royal Academy in 1897. The animal skin helps identify the god while giving a cast viewer another texture and contour against which to judge his body. The animal skin on the right shoulder interrupts the clean fall of the standing figure’s outline. Its folds draw attention to the smooth, extended planes of the chest and legs.

The North Carolina Museum of Art dates this marble to the first century CE. An earlier identification as an emperor in the guise of Jupiter remains a historical reading of the work. The surviving edge of the mantle offers evidence for the arrangement of a statue whose limbs and setting are otherwise lost. The muscular torso rises above heavy cloth gathered at the hips. The change from the broad chest to closely layered folds gives the fragment a strong visual hinge.

This marble torso comes from a Roman version of the resting satyr associated with Praxiteles. The panther skin helps identify the figure despite the loss of its head and limbs. The survival of the animal skin gives a fragment the kind of iconographic evidence that a bare torso often lacks. Follow the panther skin where it crosses the chest and catches at the waist. Its diagonal brings out the slack, sideways shift of the torso.

This first- or second-century Roman marble in Copenhagen belongs to the Aphrodite Pudica type. The goddess is shown after bathing, beside a water jar and cloak. The arrangement belongs to a family of images in which the goddess’s gesture governs what the viewer is allowed to see from each side. Look at the relationship between the torso and the structure at its side. The original covering gesture is part of a composition that repeatedly directs attention toward the areas it would shield.

This Roman marble follows Myron’s Discobolus and dates to the second century CE. The fragment was found in the River Aude in the eighteenth century and is now at the Musée Saint-Raymond. The torso remains evidence for the circulation of the discus-throwing type, even after the characteristic apparatus and extended limbs have disappeared. The shortened shoulder and hip lines still suggest the torque of a throw. View the fragment obliquely to see how much action survives in the planes of the torso alone.

The Hunt Museum dates this surviving white marble male torso to the sixteenth century. The fragmentary state leaves its original subject open. The fragment permits study of Renaissance modeling while its missing parts prevent it from securing a more specific original identity. The chest retains a subtle turn across the abdomen, while the cut edges and losses interrupt that movement. From the side, the depth of the rib cage becomes more evident.

This 2002 plaster cast reproduces one of Michelangelo’s unfinished marble Captives, carved around 1530–34 for the project of Julius II’s tomb. The original’s unworked stone is part of what the cast preserves. A modern museum cast transmits a body from a project with an unusually complex history of planning, carving, and dispersal. The turn of the rib cage seems to continue into the block. In an oblique view, roughness gathers around the figure’s outline and makes the release of a shoulder or hip feel partial.

Adriaen de Vries made this bronze in 1593 during his Prague period. It shows Mercury carrying Psyche aloft, a subject that puts flight and physical support into the same composition. The subject makes a difficult casting problem meaningful because the appearance of flight depends on minimizing the visual weight of the joined figures. Follow the upward spiral from Mercury’s stance to the figures’ meeting arms. From one side Psyche’s weight seems suspended, and from another the points of support become clear.

Pierre Puget carved this Carrara marble for Versailles, and Louis XIV accepted it in 1684. The subject is Perseus’s rescue of Andromeda from a sea monster. Puget’s rescue scene uses several bodies to give a turning view of an action in progress, a central problem for sculpture in the round. Look from the rocks and sea debris upward through the body and the drapery. The group keeps changing direction as it rises, and its silhouette opens at different points as you turn it.

In this eighteenth-century marble, John Bacon gives the Roman god of war the idealized body of British Neoclassical sculpture. The Usher Gallery holds the version shown here. The Roman war god was a familiar academic subject, but Bacon’s handling helps distinguish this particular eighteenth-century treatment from an antique model. The upright figure is steadied visually by the tree support and sword. The bend of the arm behind his hip introduces a turn within that firm vertical arrangement.

Claude Poirier carved Arethusa between 1706 and 1711 for the royal gardens of Marly. In myth, the nymph becomes a spring, making her an apt subject for a water feature. The stream or spring associated with Arethusa gives the nymph’s figure a particular place within the classical language of water imagery. Compare the slow turn of the upper body with the faster ripples of the carved cloth. The folds draw the eye along the extended figure and across the base.

This lead figure follows Georg Raphael Donner’s fountain sculpture in Vienna and dates to after 1739. The attribution to Jakob Gabriel Mollinarolo remains tentative. Lead allowed this composition to travel in a different material from its monumental precedent, with consequences for the definition of small details. Follow the nymph’s turn toward the dog. Its small upright shape gives the eye a point of rest against the length of the reclining body.

Stanley modeled Amor Patriae in 1777, making love of country an allegory embodied by a classical figure. Sword and laurel give it a civic vocabulary of duty and honor. A moral concept becomes visible through a body and an attribute, as in many eighteenth-century academic allegories. The sword extends the figure’s stance downward while the wreath concentrates attention near the hand. Lightly gathered cloth leaves the line through chest and legs clear.

John Bacon the Elder’s Coade stone river god was purchased in 1781 for the Duke of Montagu’s gardens at Buccleuch House. It was later moved to Richmond Terrace Gardens. The Coade manufacture links allegorical garden sculpture to the eighteenth-century production of durable figures for outdoor settings. The bearded figure’s long recumbent pose shares the width of the plinth. One arm props the torso, giving a human body the broad, low presence of a river.

The inscription on this nineteenth-century marble records Gibson’s work in Rome. The classical subject is treated as a quiet moment before bathing. A nymph preparing to bathe is part of a sculptural convention in which an everyday action gives an ideal nude a reason to move. The head turns away from the direction of the knees. Drapery gathers across the lap and rock while the small vessel locates the body in the act of preparing to bathe.

Pradier exhibited this marble at the Salon of 1819 as Une Nymphe. Its identification as a follower of Bacchus took hold soon afterward. Its two titles let the same reclining body shift from a broad category of nature spirit to a participant in bacchic mythology. A hand drawn across one breast follows the larger turn of the reclining torso. The pose leads the eye obliquely across the figure.

John Gibson’s Venus belongs to nineteenth-century Neoclassicism. The apple recalls the prize Paris awarded the goddess, and a tortoise accompanies her at the feet. Gibson’s particular title gives the goddess a power over human feeling and changes how an otherwise familiar antique nude is encountered. The hand holding the apple brings the gesture close to the torso. Compare that compact upper silhouette with the longer line of the figure and the folds around her lower body.

David d’Angers’s 1837 marble depicts the Greek general Philopoemen removing a weapon from his leg. The elaborately worked armor places the moment of injury in a martial setting. The military narrative is made visible through a contained gesture, concentrating attention on the body’s effort instead of illustrating a battle. The bent torso directs the eye toward the wound. Turn the sculpture to compare the sweep of the shield and helmet with the tight line of the reaching arm.

Mariemont's historical guide records this marble by Simonis in 1852. Its two titles identify the figure as Truth Unveiled or as the muse Thalia. The alternative titles show how an exposed or unveiled figure could circulate between several allegorical interpretations. The cloth falls as the figure draws it across the body. The contrast between the folds and the exposed torso makes unveiling the sculpture's central action.

Chauncey Bradley Ives shows the water spirit Undine emerging with her arms raised. The marble alternates between drapery that clings to the figure and folds that gather above her head. That contrast makes the rising figure readable in silhouette and suggests cloth saturated with water.

Alfred Boucher’s 1892 marble entered the French national collection the year it was made. It has been on deposit at Pau since 1978. Its early acquisition and provincial deposit show how a Salon-era marble could pass from production into the French public collections. The elbows open while the body extends across the cushioned support. The low profile makes small changes in the height of the knees and shoulders especially noticeable.

Tegner’s 1899 original plaster was shown at the 1900 Paris exhibition. Later marble and bronze monuments are separate versions of this memorial. The original plaster documents the design before later monumental versions, so its scale, material and exhibition history matter in their own right. The woman’s back emerges from the rough surround, directing attention to the turn of her body away from the viewer. The contrast in modeling makes that withdrawal feel physical.

Vermare made these marble personifications of the Rhône and Saône in 1905 for the steps of Lyon's Palais de la Bourse. The intertwined figures represent the meeting of the city's two rivers. The figures use a familiar allegorical language to make a city’s rivers legible as bodies within the architecture of a civic building. Follow the point where the two bodies touch and see how the surrounding water carries their movement outward. The confluence takes shape through contact between the figures.

Bock carved this group in shell limestone in 1912. The three women at Hamburg's Sievekingplatz personify the Hanseatic cities of Bremen, Hamburg and Lübeck. The three cities become distinct bodies in a civic allegory, allowing architectural ornament to speak through the arrangement of a group. A seated, a kneeling and a reclining figure share one support. Follow the changes in height across the group before looking at how their bodies link together.

The French state purchased Béclu's marble group in 1913. It stands in Lyon's Parc de la Tête d'Or. The state purchase and park installation place an intimate figure group in a civic setting where the title can color an encounter with it. The figures' bodies turn toward one another as a secret passes between them. From outside the group, the closeness of the heads and shoulders makes their conversation feel private.

The scan publisher identifies this bronze near Vienna's former ministry entrance at Radetzkystraße 2 as Hanak's The Burning Man and dates the composition to 1922. The casting date is unconfirmed. Its allegorical title directs attention to the body as a vehicle for feeling instead of identifying the sculpture as a portrait. The upraised arms carry the upright body higher. Look at how the urgent lift of the gesture gives force to the title.

Maillol’s composition dates to 1925. The Harvard bronze records that standing figure, but the date of this casting has yet to be verified. The place name turns an observed body into an allegorical figure, a recurring relationship between Maillol’s models and his titles. The cloth held behind the hips draws the shoulders back and opens the chest. The faint curve through the back becomes clearest in profile.

Callender’s c. 1930 granite torso makes the partial figure a self-contained modern sculpture. The work entered the Smithsonian American Art Museum through Harold Callender’s bequest. Using granite for a self-contained torso puts the density of the material in conversation with the modern practice of making fragments intentional. From the back, the shoulders taper into the waist before opening again at the hips. The continuous modeling keeps the eye moving across the simplified stone.

The City of Paris dates Valsamis's La Pureté to 1955 and records it in the upper part of Parc Montsouris. The bronze's casting date is unrecorded. As a municipal sculpture it offers an abstract moral idea in the familiar visual terms of a standing figure. The head inclines as the arms descend close to the torso. The slight crossing of the legs gathers the figure over its shaped base.

Andrien modeled Le Nanti in plaster in 1973 and cast it in bronze in 1975. The Sart Tilman open-air museum received it on deposit in 1987. The passage from plaster model to open-air bronze connects studio modeling with the changed light and scale of a public site. The man occupies two chairs, with his arms and legs spread and his belly projecting forward. The expansiveness makes the pose a satire of complacency.

Winebaum made this bronze in 2002. The University of New Hampshire records exhibitions of it in 2008 and 2012. The wall belongs to the subject and to the arrangement of the figure, making a barrier part of the composition itself. The hands rise into space as if it were a solid plane. The forward lean makes the absent wall legible through the body's balance.

Eskridge’s aluminum Torso Fragment dates to 2005 and was given by the artist to Indiana University. Its hollow body and cut-off limbs deliberately quote the appearance of an antique fragment. A work titled as a fragment can evoke ancient survival even when its cropping and finish are choices made by a living sculptor. The twist through chest and hips carries the classical stance. The open ends reveal the thinness of the metal shell, changing the torso’s appearance as it turns.

The Musée Cognacq-Jay attributes this small marble to Joseph or Ignace Broche. An earlier attribution gave it to Étienne-Maurice Falconet. The attribution to two possible makers distinguishes what is known about the sculptural type from what is known about this particular object. The foot set across the opposite knee draws her arms and gaze down into a tight knot. Follow the diagonal of the raised shin to see how much of the pose comes from that simple act of drying a foot.

The scan records this almost life-size Baroque Venus in Vienna, with maker and precise date unrecorded. Shell and dolphins connect the garden-scale figure to her birth from the sea. The shell places Venus within a well-established iconography of birth and sea, a subject particularly suited to sculptural display near water. The shell broadens the base and the dolphins set up smaller curves below the standing body. That contrast makes the vertical figure read as a lift from the water.

This figure represents Amphitrite, ruler of the sea, within the classical company of the Slavkov Palace gardens. The attribution and date are unrecorded. The sea goddess belongs to a long tradition of water figures used to link garden sculpture with the place in which it is seen. A turned head and gathered cloth at the hip enliven the upright pose. The edge between the bare torso and cascading folds holds the eye around the statue’s middle.

This statue is identified in the scan as a naiad, a freshwater nymph, in the Slavkov Palace gardens. The source leaves the maker and date open. The title identifies a conventional water spirit and leaves the sculptor and date of this particular park figure unrecorded. The volute under the figure follows the curve of its posture. Its more emphatic spiral steadies the diagonal of the body and gives the whole arrangement a rising movement.

This Berlin-made plaster, acquired by SMK in 1897, follows the Fontainebleau bronze adaptation of the Vatican Sleeping Ariadne. The chain of versions records how a classical figure moved between collections and materials. A nineteenth-century cast made through a Renaissance bronze records how the sleeping Ariadne composition was translated across periods and materials. The elbow rising behind the head gives the reclining silhouette its highest point. From there, folds run down the body and lengthen the impression of sleep.

Jacques Guillemot’s stone sculpture in the Waux-Hall park uses the torso as a modern figurative subject. The record gives no creation date. A torso with an independent title invites comparison with modern sculpture’s use of the fragment as an intended form. The reclining body reads first as broad, adjoining volumes. Turn it to see how the raised torso and low, sweeping mass of the hips pull in different directions.

This torso is documented in the sculpture park on Kant Island in Kaliningrad. Its maker and date remain unrecorded. The site identifies the recorded object more securely than its title can establish a maker, date or original commission. The tall pedestal narrows the field of attention to a small shift of weight at the waist. Compare its rigid vertical with the changing outline of the body above.

Romania’s National Institute of Heritage identifies this small plaster as a classicizing work by Ion Irimescu. The date and holding collection are unrecorded. Even with the date unknown, the survival of a small plaster makes it possible to examine how this artist used an antique-looking fragment. With the head and limbs absent, the modeling of the chest, waist, and hips carries the figure. Turn from the front to the side to see how the weight shifts across those curves.

This patinated plaster torso relates to Rodin’s Gates of Hell. The scan was made while the work was on view in a British Museum exhibition. Rodin’s torso shows how a figure conceived in motion could acquire a second life as an independent composition. The chest arches backward, stretching the surface above the abdomen. With the limbs gone, that bend provides the strongest clue to the force acting on the body.

The unsigned bronze carries a label naming A. Nelson. The scan publisher treats it as a later work in Anton Nelson's Art Nouveau manner, with the maker and date unconfirmed. The unsigned object can be compared with Art Nouveau’s use of plant motifs while the label alone leaves authorship unsettled. The lifted leaf directs attention back toward the face. Its small gesture gives a point of focus to the full-length standing figure.

Cleveland now identifies this small Greek bronze of about 510–500 BCE as probably Herakles. That reading takes the raised arm to be part of a striking gesture. Its small scale gives an impression of action very different from the later monumental versions through which Herakles is often recognized. The stride turns the torso even with both hands and parts of the feet lost. The carefully arranged hair provides a dense counterpoint to the figure’s broad muscular planes.

SMK’s cast follows the Farnese Diadumenos, a Roman marble in the British Museum. Scholars have debated the Greek prototype’s relationship to Polykleitos and Pheidias. A ribbon-binding gesture is recognizably athletic yet ordinary, a useful case of ancient sculptors making nobility from a modest action. The athlete lifts a victory ribbon to his head, opening two clear spaces beneath his elbows. The legs shift their weight below, so the raised arms never produce a rigid symmetry.

This plaster in SMK’s Royal Cast Collection reproduces a figure long called the Belvedere Antinous, now generally identified as Hermes. The cast’s maker and date are unknown. The change in title is evidence of reception because the same idealized body carried both a named historical identity and a divine reading. From the front, the weight settles onto one leg and the other foot eases back. The inclination of the head follows the softening of the figure’s stance.

SMK acquired this plaster cast in 1901. Its Roman marble prototype in the Louvre preserves a Late Classical Greek type associated with the Lyceum in Athens and the style of Praxiteles. The cast transmits an ancient composition through at least two acts of copying, each in a different setting from the Greek prototype. The arm laid over the head establishes a recognizable gesture of rest. Turn the model to follow the relaxed shift in weight between the figure and the support.

This SMK Royal Cast Collection plaster reproduces the Capitoline Venus type, known through a Roman marble after a Hellenistic original. A plaster replica preserves the organization of the Roman model while replacing its marble surface with the relatively even finish of a cast. Compare the two protective gestures, one across the chest and one at the pelvis. From the side their curves have an echo in the shift of the weight-bearing hip.

SMK acquired this plaster cast in 1898. The Louvre prototype has been called Germanicus, and SMK also records the possibility that the standing figure represents Octavian. The acquisition of a cast records how a museum collected a historically influential pose even while its sitter remained in dispute. One hand lifts beside the face while a length of drapery falls from the other arm. These gestures frame the nude torso with two very different vertical lines.

This Roman marble, made between 27 BCE and 68 CE, adapts the Greek sculptor Polykleitos's Spear Bearer. The Minneapolis example is a separate ancient sculpture from the Naples marble known through casts. A Roman marble version is evidence of the circulation of a Greek sculptural model whose original bronze is no longer available. Follow the weight down the supporting leg, then up through the shift of the hips. The corresponding change across the shoulders gives the still figure a sense of motion.

Nationalmuseum identifies this bronze as Giambologna’s Neptune. It once belonged to the architect Nicodemus Tessin the Younger, and the date of this casting is unrecorded. Small bronzes after Giambologna could circulate without their own casting dates being documented, an important distinction in crediting the model and present object. One leg bends as the arms reach in opposing directions. Rotating the model makes the balance between the sea god’s planted weight and his outward gesture easier to see.

The helmeted warrior reproduces figure IX of the west pediment of the Temple of Aphaia, dated about 500–490 BCE. SMK acquired this plaster in 1952. The figure’s shield and lower pose show how the triangle of a temple pediment shaped the depiction of a body in battle. The circular shield creates a clear field behind the bent limbs. The raised arm and planted feet set a more angular pattern against the shield’s curve.

This cast follows a Roman marble derived from a Greek composition dated around 440 BCE. The traditional name Munich King gives the figure its catalog identity while the sitter remains unidentified. The historic name Munich King illustrates how an inherited title can survive even after the identity of the person becomes uncertain. The tree trunk and cloth build a secondary vertical beside the standing nude. Compare that upright support with the small shifts through the man’s knees, hips and shoulders.

The scan publisher identifies this reclining nymph as a second-century Roman marble in Copenhagen’s Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek. The accession and exact institutional identification remain unconfirmed. A reclining nymph belongs to a repertory of antique water figures in which sleep allows a long horizontal composition. The propped torso rises from a long, draped stretch of legs. Look at the shallow slope between shoulder and hip, which gives the reclining pose some tension.

This second-century Roman marble takes its pose from the Aphrodite of Knidos, Praxiteles’ celebrated Greek image of the goddess. Its surface bears the effects of prolonged outdoor exposure. The work illustrates the reach of the Knidian type through Roman copying, which preserved a celebrated composition without preserving its original marble. The slight shift of the hips remains legible through the weathering. Compare the softened details of the surface with the clear contour of the body as you turn it.

Three D Scans recorded this first- or second-century Roman marble at National Museums Liverpool. The catalog preserves the title Sleeping Venus. The old title supplies a tradition of interpretation, while the pose itself belongs to a much wider antique repertory of reclining figures. From the long side, follow the figure’s reclining outline from lifted upper body through the legs. The thin support emphasizes the low height and extended width of the pose.

This second-century Roman torso from the gymnasium at Salamis follows a Greek statue type. The Fitzwilliam Museum records the marble as possibly Parian. The findspot and ancient date anchor the fragment historically even though much of its original identifying detail is lost. The material gathered high around the shoulder gives the remaining chest a dense, uneven border. The smooth modeling across the front makes the turn easier to trace.

The work represented here is a plaster cast in SMK’s Royal Cast Collection. Its antique prototype portrays Antinous, the companion of Emperor Hadrian whose image circulated widely after his death. Antinous was widely represented in antiquity, and the cast preserves this one treatment of the balance between individual identity and an ideal body. The slight turn of the head opposes the shift at the hips. Follow that change of direction through the shoulders and on down to the relaxed foot.

This Roman Imperial marble reworks an early Hellenistic composition. Found on Rome’s Caelian Hill in 1608, the group was extensively restored by Nicolas Cordier the following year. Cordier’s restoration belongs to an early modern history of the group and complicates treating the surviving arrangement as exclusively antique. The middle Grace turns her back to the viewer while her companions face forward, linking the three bodies across their shoulders. Turn the group to see that exchange of fronts and backs reverse.

This small Bacchus is a fourth-century figure carved in Göktepe marble. It belongs to the Musée Saint-Raymond in Toulouse. The late-antique date places this image within the continued reuse of established divine types across changing Roman contexts. Look at the mass of the hair and the angle of the head against the comparatively smooth torso. The surviving shoulder and thigh stumps mark the limits of what the fragment can tell us about the pose.

Michelangelo carved David from a single block of marble in 1501–1504. The figure stood outside Florence's Palazzo della Signoria before being moved to the Accademia. Placing the figure in a civic square made a biblical subject into a public image of vigilance and authority. The hand carrying the sling lifts toward the shoulder, while the other hangs open beside the thigh. Their different levels of tension make the hero look poised before action.

Michelangelo carved the original marble for the tomb of Julius II in the 1510s. The scan shows the SMK Royal Cast Collection plaster. The cast carries a tomb figure into a teaching and museum setting where viewers can study the spiraling pose at close range. One arm lifts over the head while a narrow band crosses the chest. Compare the relaxed bend of the figure with the small signs of restraint.

This 1898 plaster cast in SMK's Royal Cast Collection reproduces Michelangelo's marble Apollo, carved around 1530. The Renaissance date refers to the original. The name Apollo is an interpretation of the marble, and the cast allows its unresolved subject and unfinished form to be examined together. The rising elbow, bowed head and crossed legs wind the body into a spiral. The pose reads especially clearly when seen from the side.

The Minneapolis Institute of Art catalogs this seventeenth-century bronze as the work of Pierre Puget. The bow recasts the familiar Hercules as a figure of aim and control. An archer’s indirect relationship to a target makes the unseen space outside the statue part of its composition. Trace the arc of the bow beside the twists of the shoulders and chest. The drawing arm folds close to the face while the bow projects beyond the figure’s compact outline.

This standing Venus brings a classical subject into the palace gardens at Slavkov. The scan publisher attributes it to Giovanni Giuliani and dates it to 1700, with the exact version unconfirmed. The garden setting places the statue in the tradition of using classical figures to punctuate walks and views through a designed landscape. The turn of the upper body draws the eye into the drapery gathered at one side. The cloth’s folds give the smooth torso a more distinct outline.

Nollekens’s marble Mercury belongs to eighteenth-century British Neoclassicism. The inscription records the Earl of Yarborough’s gift to the Usher Gallery in 1930. Putting Mercury beside Bacon’s Mars shows how two British Neoclassical sculptors distinguished divine identities through differing attitudes and attributes. The winged helmet draws the eye to the head. Below it, drapery crosses the hips and connects the bare limbs and chest to the rocky seat.

This stone Hercules at the Royal Łazienki Museum probably dates to the eighteenth century. Wiesław Winkler restored the missing head, using a museum employee as the model. The replacement of the head is part of the object’s history and limits how confidently the present expression can be read as original. Follow the arms as they open the lion’s jaws, then trace the strain back through Hercules’s chest and stance. The lion gives the hero’s effort a fixed point of resistance.

The Schönbrunn garden Apollo is identified as a marble by Johann Baptist Hagenauer, dated 1779 by the scan publisher. The tree and coiled Python set the myth of Apollo’s victory in view. An outdoor Apollo can organize a sightline as much as represent a god, a useful way to read this figure within the palace grounds. The archer’s extended arm draws the eye away from the trunk. Python’s coils offer a tighter pattern beside that open gesture and lead the eye back into the statue.

Christian Gottfried Jüchtzer devised this faun for Meissen in 1783–1784. The manufactory produced this porcelain example between 1784 and 1814. Porcelain moves the antique dancing figure into the sphere of the display cabinet, giving its movement a smaller and more intimate scale. The dipped head and bent knee interrupt the upright line of the body. The tilt suggests a beat, turning a gesture associated with music into a visible rhythm.

Göthe carved this Bacchus in Rome in 1808, following his training with Canova. The cup and panther skin identify the wine god within a restrained Neoclassical composition. The wine god belongs to a Neoclassical repertory in which antique deities also became studies of softness, finish and balance. The panther skin gathers beside the seated body and gives the marble a more broken surface. The relaxed torso and small gesture of the cup balance that texture.

This nineteenth-century plaster in Denmark’s Royal Cast Collection reproduces Canova’s Venus Italica, completed in marble in 1812. The pose carries an antique vocabulary of modesty into the early nineteenth century and makes protection of the body an active gesture. Move from the gathered cloth at the front to the exposed back. The shift of weight toward one hip becomes especially clear from behind.

This marble in Monaco is one version of François-Joseph Bosio’s Salmacis. The Louvre holds a related marble, commissioned in 1826 and completed in 1836. Salmacis belongs to a classical story of desire and bodily transformation, but the individual figure can suggest that narrative through pose alone. The folded legs collect the composition close to the ground while the shoulders and head turn away. From the side, the pose reads as a controlled rise from the support through the back.

Thorvaldsen's 1803 model won him a commission from Thomas Hope and helped establish his reputation. The marble, delivered in 1828, later gave Elmgreen & Dragset a starting point for Jason (Briefs). Hope’s commission is part of the work’s history as an internationally patronized statement of the new classicism. Compare the fleece's hanging folds with the long, uninterrupted line of the standing figure. The body's composure makes the prize feel like the aftermath of action.

Denis Foyatier carved this marble in 1830. By giving the rebellious Spartacus the monumental form of an academic nude, he presents resistance through the figure’s bearing. The subject gives a body of the kind taught in academies a modern political charge through its identification with an enslaved rebel. Follow the relation between the upper limbs and the firm line of the stance. The body remains exposed even as its upright posture asserts control.

This nineteenth-century plaster teaching cast was probably made in Kraków after an earlier academy cast. It reproduces the ancient type of a satyr playing cymbals and working a foot-operated clapper, or scabellum. A nineteenth-century teaching cast is evidence of how the dancing satyr entered the study of antique figure conventions outside Italy. The arms strike out at different heights as the torso tilts over the legs. Look down at the feet to see how the rhythm in the upper body continues into the base.

Bissen modeled Achilles in 1861 and carved this marble between 1864 and 1866. He takes the subject from the quarrel over Briseis in the Iliad. The subject turns a literary episode into a study of how a figure can appear to restrain anger while remaining almost still. The seated pose keeps Achilles in place while his taut body suggests an urge to move. Look at how the gathered limbs hold the anger close to the torso.

Howard Roberts made this marble in 1873–76. Its title suggests a model’s first pose, making the studio encounter part of the subject. The studio is the implied context of the pose, making attention to modeling and the relationship between sculptor and sitter part of the subject. The torso turns toward the raised arm while the cloth descends along the chair. The figure’s polished surface and the deeper creases of the fabric separate the body from its support.

Rodin conceived Adam in 1880–1881 and proposed placing it beside The Gates of Hell. Its pose draws on Michelangelo's depiction of Adam in the Sistine Chapel. The Michelangelo reference is a case of Rodin translating an earlier image into the weight and viewpoint of a figure in the round. The lowered head and hand pointing toward the ground draw the body down into a twist. The heavy musculature gives that inward gesture considerable force.

Leighton developed the figure in 1885, bringing an everyday stretch into the repertoire of the Victorian nude. This scan captures the Royal Academy’s version, whose medium remains unverified. An ordinary stretch becomes the subject of a monumental figure, showing the late Victorian interest in recasting everyday movement as sculpture. The bent elbows pull the gaze up along the ribs. A slight shift at the hips keeps the long body from settling into a straight line.

Rodin’s reduced Eve derives from his 1881 model. The scan identifies this marble as an 1892 execution of a version reduced in 1883. Reduction is part of Rodin’s treatment of the figure because changing the scale gives a familiar pose a new viewing distance. Follow the line down the back from the hunched shoulders to the hips. Turning to the front reveals the arms folded tightly across the chest.

SMK acquired this undated plaster cast in 1896. It follows a Roman marble copy of the fifth-century BCE Doryphoros, or spear bearer, associated with Polykleitos. A nineteenth-century cast preserves an example of how sculptors and students learned Polykleitan balance through later copies. The straight standing leg and the relaxed leg make the hips tilt. Follow the opposing tilt of the shoulders to see how the figure achieves balance through asymmetry.

Rodin developed this deliberately truncated figure around 1896–97. Alexis Rudier cast the V&A bronze, which Rodin gave to the museum in 1914. The title suggests music or inspiration while the truncated figure shows how Rodin could communicate through a body with very few narrative attributes. The bowed head brings the movement back into the body. With the arms absent, the bend at the waist and the twist through the ribs carry much of the gesture.

This plaster cast entered SMK's Royal Cast Collection in 1897. Its Vatican prototype was celebrated by Johann Joachim Winckelmann and widely copied for centuries. Winckelmann’s reception of the Apollo belongs to the history of the cast because that critical fame helped make the type worth replicating. Apollo's head turns away from the line of his extended arm. The cloak carries that gesture outward before falling in folds beside the open torso.

Rodin’s Psyche was shown in Paris in 1900. The myth supplies the scene of Psyche trying to see her sleeping lover. The story of Psyche lends emotional suggestions to the body, giving the pose a role that exceeds any literal identification by attributes. Her body pitches forward beneath the cloak. The folds and roughly worked base retain a broad sweep around the more delicately modeled figure.

The scan publisher attributes this early twentieth-century outdoor bronze to Anton Hanak. It stands left of the former ministry entrance at Radetzkystraße 2, Vienna. The tentative identification and unconsolidated cast history are worth keeping separate from what can be seen in the public bronze. The hands come together near the chest and concentrate movement in the upper body. Seen from the side, the compact gesture changes the outline of the standing figure.

SMK acquired this plaster cast in 1904 under the historic title Dying Gladiator. It follows the Capitoline Dying Gaul, a Roman version of a Hellenistic composition. The change from Gladiator to Gaul is a history of interpretation in which attributes and bodily presentation have carried different meanings. The propped arm bears most of the upper body’s weight, leaving the long diagonal of the legs close to the ground. The lowered head brings the figure’s energy back toward the base.

Octobre carved this marble in 1906. It is on deposit from the Musée d'Orsay at Montmorillon, which also holds a bronze statuette of the subject. The coexistence of marble and bronze versions makes material a part of the work’s history rather than an incidental description. The head and upper body incline as the nymph studies her reflection. The downward gesture gives an implied location to the water.

Bugatti conceived the seated figure in 1907. The Gravelines bronze is a posthumous cast dated 1990 on its plaque, which names the C. Valsuani foundry. The posthumous casting date matters because a work experienced as public sculpture today is the afterlife of a much earlier design. One arm rests across a raised knee while the other takes weight against the rock seat. The lowered head gathers this large body into a close, inward composition.

The Musée Bourdelle identifies this plaster as the full-scale model for the second version of Hercules the Archer, dated 1909–23. A working model preserves the full span of Bourdelle’s composition. Bourdelle’s second version shows how refining a related figure can change the problem of tension across its body and its surrounding space. The upper body stretches nearly sideways as the limbs brace against the rock. The great arc of the bow holds open a space that would disappear in a more compact pose.

Wouters made this composition, also known as La Joie de vivre, in 1912. Dr Désiré Jaumain donated the Colonster bronze to the University of Liège collection in 1972. The title invokes a figurative tradition, while the buoyancy of the moving body does much of the work of departure from it. One foot carries the figure while the lifted knee and extended arms spread its movement outward. Follow the figure from the supporting foot up through the open arms.

Maillol commemorated Cézanne with an idealized reclining woman holding a palm. This lead version in the Jardin du Carrousel replaces the original stone monument. A monument to a painter is expressed through a human figure, an example of how public commemoration can work through allegory. The upper body rises briefly before the legs draw the composition back down into a long horizontal. The held palm arrests the eye midway along that line and gives the repose the character of an offering.

Desenfans made this bronze in 1913. Its biblical subject and full-length nude share a public setting in Parc Josaphat, Schaerbeek. The serpent makes an abstract moral choice visible through a figure’s bodily relation to an animal and the directions of its gestures. Read the vertical line of Eve's standing body alongside the serpent's form. The two contours hold the figures of the story together.

The scan publisher dates this Hanak composition to 1915 and locates the bronze left of the former ministry entrance at Radetzkystraße 2, Vienna. The casting date remains unconfirmed. The architectural setting gives the figure a civic visibility that differs from the intimate viewing conditions of a small studio nude. The torso rises away from the reclining body and both arms extend overhead. The gesture gives the figure a long diagonal when seen from the side.

The documentation accompanying the scan identifies this white-stone bather as a 1925 work by Germaine Marboutier, held in Pau. The bather’s ordinary activity gives a reason for turning and folding the body that carries no mythological narrative. From behind, the rise of the back and the turn of the head stand out against the broad stone base. The horizontal support gives the small changes in direction their clarity.

Marès made this bronze in 1926. The Museu de l'Empordà documents it in Figueres. The date places this figure within a twentieth-century continuation of the academy nude, where the use of a historical genre can itself be a choice. The torso and legs make a compact standing figure. Follow the narrowing at the waist and the way the model's mass opens again at the hips.

The Louvre dates this lead group in the Jardin du Carrousel to 1930. Maillol reworks the classical Three Graces as a rhythm of three standing figures. Maillol returned to an antique group type that offered a way to test how much variation could be created from three similar bodies. Walk around the group to see which figures overlap and which separate. Each changes the direction of shoulders and hips just enough to prevent the three bodies from reading as a repeated outline.

Wlérick developed L'Offrande between 1932 and 1937. The bronze at Pont Gisèle Halimi in Mont-de-Marsan stands near his separate composition La Jeunesse. The title casts the action as a presentation, directing the viewer to read gesture in relation to the body that supports it. The outstretched gesture carries the eye from the center of the figure into surrounding space. In the round, the offering reads as much through its direction as through the body.

Wlérick began Rolande in 1937 and showed a full-size plaster in 1943. This scan records the half-size bronze in the Musée Despiau-Wlérick, whose casting date remains unconfirmed. The half-size cast records one scale of an evolving project and changes how a viewer judges the body’s mass and surroundings. Small shifts across the shoulders and hips hold the standing figure in balance. Looking closely, the pose's quietness makes those adjustments easier to see.

Charles Despiau based his standing nude on the professional model Assia Granatouroff. The Middelheim bronze featured in the museum’s first exhibition in 1950 and was acquired the following year. The named figure lets a viewer consider how a modern sculptor moved between individual likeness and the long tradition of the standing nude. Start from the back, where the shoulders and hips are slightly out of line. The close-set legs and arms keep the figure compact, so a small turn of the head makes a pronounced change in direction.

SMK acquired this undated plaster cast in 1939. It reproduces the Greek bronze from Cape Artemision, generally dated to around 460–450 BCE and identified as either Zeus or Poseidon. The absent weapon leaves the god’s name open while showing how sculptural movement can still be read from the hand and extended arms. Seen head-on, the reach of the arms is balanced by the wide stance. From the side, the shoulders and hips reveal the turn needed to throw the lost weapon.

Kolbe developed this composition in 1939–1941. The bronze was erected in Berlin’s Georg-Kolbe-Hain in 1965. The passage from composition to outdoor erection puts the present object in a different historical moment from the first design. The supporting elbow carries the upper body while the legs fold back toward it. Seen from the side, that arrangement creates a long continuous curve through the torso.

Maillol worked on The River from 1939 to 1943. The Middelheim Museum’s lead version gives the force of flowing water the form of a human body. The river’s title frames the body as a natural force, with the unstable pose giving the allegory its momentum. The shoulders and hips turn on different axes as the figure stretches past its support. That slip from the base makes the weight of the body feel momentarily ungoverned.

Rivière’s 1951 reclining figure is recorded at Albi’s municipal swimming pool. The waterside subject takes on a literal setting in that civic space. Installing the figure at a pool ties the inherited reclining type to a modern public setting explicitly concerned with water. The weight passes through one propped arm, opening the chest above the low base. The raised knee interrupts the horizontal sweep and brings the eye back toward the face.

Greco made the bronze Bather No. 2 in 1957. This example is held by the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium in Brussels. The numbered title places this bronze within a series of variations on bathing, a durable subject for studying pose and balance. The arms cross the elongated torso and draw the gesture inward. Look at how little space the standing figure needs to convey the movement.

Laurent modeled this bronze Venus in 1958 for Indiana University Bloomington’s Showalter Fountain, dedicated in 1961. It is the central figure in an ensemble titled The Birth of Venus. The dedication date belongs to the fountain’s civic history and should be separated from the earlier date of Laurent’s figure. The body rises sideways out of a shell, with the arms reaching high at one end. Foreshortening compresses that sweep into a sudden lift when seen from near the feet.

Kolbe modeled the figure in 1940–1942 for an unrealized wartime memorial. H. Noack cast this Berlin bronze in 1961. The later cast preserves a wartime composition whose original monument was never executed, changing its setting and public address. The knees yield as the arms reach upward. The opposing directions keep the broad chest open while drawing attention to the loss of balance below.

Fritz Pilz’s 1966 figure belongs to the continued use of the standing nude in twentieth-century Austrian sculpture. Its title identifies the pose without specifying a sitter or story. The title states pose and subject plainly, leaving the figure to be read alongside twentieth-century experiments with the traditional standing nude. The lifted elbows widen the silhouette at the shoulders. Follow the changing width down through the narrowing waist and the curve of the hips.

Jan Hána's 1977 stone sculpture is recorded on Kampa in Prague. Hána’s date places the seated nude within a continuing modern practice of studying how a body occupies the space around a support. The torso bends forward and the arms fold across the body, drawing the pose into itself. Walk around the sculpture to see how the back carries that curve.

The City of Gravelines places La Vigie above Gadenne's La Conversation in the Arsenal gardens. The 1981 date comes from the scan publisher. The title of the lookout makes viewing a reciprocal subject because the sculpture appears to watch the space a visitor occupies. The arms remain close to the body, concentrating attention on the narrow outline of the standing figure. Look at the sculpture in profile to see how much of its gesture stays within that outline.

The pedestal in Gravelines's Jardins de l'Arsenal names Magda Németh and bears the date 1991. The precise date of casting is unrecorded. The named allegory gives a freestanding body a public meaning, but the inscription is firmer evidence for its dating than the cast itself. The hands are held behind the body while the chest arches forward and the head lifts. Opposing movements meet in the steady base formed by the knees.

The scan publisher identifies this work as Ekaterina Harrison’s 1997 cast-iron Mirage. The record places the captured sculpture in Hamilton, New Jersey. The scan publisher’s dating and attribution establish a starting point while leaving the work’s commission and original display unconfirmed. The lifted torso gives a long, low silhouette its point of tension. Pale and dark areas in the captured surface change how the figure’s shallow turns read in light.

Dieckmann placed this 2008 bronze in the forecourt of St. Mary’s Church in Wismar. Its relaxed pose makes a moment of private repose part of the public space around the church tower. Naming Sofia rather than giving an allegorical title invites the viewer to consider the specificity of an individual reclining figure. The crossed legs pull the lower half together, while the planted arms raise and open the torso. Viewed from the side, the body seems to hover between those points of support.

Igor Mitoraj’s 2011 bronze in Agrigento treats Icarus as an intentionally broken figure. The work borrows the appearance of archaeological survival for a contemporary sculpture. A deliberate fragment can evoke the archaeological survival of ancient sculpture while the date keeps this object firmly in a contemporary practice. The wing extends the outline away from the low, grounded body. Walk around the edges to see where the figure pulls together and where its broken form refuses a continuous silhouette.

Bill Mack’s bonded-bronze Radiance belongs to the Miami-Dade Public Library’s art collection. The library describes its bronze-brown figure against a dark green ground. The work’s identification should rest on its source record, while its formal relationship to relief can be judged directly from the model. A raised arm extends the long line of the reclining nude. Color and relief depth work together, helping the body appear to push out from the rectangular panel.

This Slavkov garden Apollo is attributed to Giovanni Giuliani by the scan publisher. Its date and material remain unconfirmed. Its attribution remains provisional, but its place in the garden preserves a viewing relationship that an isolated digital sculpture can obscure. The statue turns across the base, with folds gathering around one hip. From an angle, the sweep of drapery and the twist above it pull the eye in different directions.

Pommier's Pomona, the goddess associated with fruit and gardens, stands in Cambrai's Jardin aux Fleurs. The object's exact date and medium remain unconfirmed. Pomona’s established association with fruit and cultivation gives the figure a place within the long use of mythology for outdoor sculpture. The raised arm makes a curve around the head, while the other arm follows the standing body's vertical line. Compare the two sides of the pose from the front.

The scan publisher attributes the figure to Antoine Bourdelle and locates it at the Musée Bourdelle. The object's formal title, medium, date and accession are unconfirmed. The attribution invites comparison with Bourdelle’s figure studies, while the evidence available for this model remains the scan publisher’s identification. The torso bends over an extended leg. Compare that long reach with the concentrated mass of the upper body.

Cesare Malpieri’s Roman workshop produced this painted plaster after the ancient Terme Ruler. SMK acquired it in 1899. The workshop identification dates one stage in the transmission of an ancient bronze whose subject remains open to debate. The tall support steadies the line of the raised arm. The hand behind the back and the turn at the hips make a different silhouette visible from each side.

Walter Leitner made this copy after Anton Hanak’s plaster model. The scan gives no date for Leitner’s version. The work’s status as a copy makes it possible to study Hanak’s arrangement independently of the history of the particular object scanned. Seen from behind, the bowed head lowers the line of the upper back. From the front, the arms drawn inward make the title’s sense of withdrawal visible in the pose.

René Harvent’s life-size bronze stands near the entrance to the Waux-Hall park in Mons. Its creation date is unrecorded. The sun supplies a setting for the pose through the title, directing attention to patterns of exposure and shelter across the body. Look at the turn from the hips into the upper back. A bent elbow and a hand laid against the body alternately widen and close the outline.

Hermida’s Venus in the Sun stands near the blue bridge in Chiclana de la Frontera. The work uses the classical name for a seated figure enjoying an ordinary sensation. The title brings an inherited goddess into a setting defined by light and exposure, even though the scan alone cannot establish the commission. The lifted face draws attention upward from the wide mass of the torso and thighs. The straight edges of the plinth emphasize the figure’s curves and the ease of her seat.

The scan credits Guy van den Steen de Jehay with this seated figure at the Château de Jehay. Neither the sculpture’s date nor its material is specified in the source. The everyday subject gives a reason for the figure’s bearing and places bodily study within a recognizable environment. The extended arm continues the direction of the gutter, while the legs drop away from its straight edge. The scan’s untextured surface makes that contrast of body and architecture especially clear.

This small Etruscan bronze once crowned an apparatus for kottabos, a drinking game played by throwing wine dregs at a balanced dish. The dish and taller support have been lost. The figure still makes sense as a participant in a drinking culture whose games and objects often borrowed the motions of mythic revelers. The satyr balances on one foot with a hand raised toward the missing dish. The pierced ring below frames a pose that seems as precarious as the game itself.

The model records Denmark’s Royal Cast Collection plaster after the late Hellenistic marble in Munich’s Glyptothek, dated in Atrium’s catalog to around 220 BCE. The figure’s sleep belongs to a Hellenistic interest in states that loosen the controlled bearing of a standing god or athlete. One arm falls over the support while the other curves above the head. The spread of the thighs keeps the sleeping figure’s weight and exposure visible from the front.

This plaster in Denmark’s Royal Cast Collection preserves a faun type dated in Atrium’s catalog to around 200 BCE. Cast collections preserve the circulation of antique poses as well as their forms. Here, the bent knee and dipped head move the body forward against the upright support. From the side, the compressed waist on one flank and the longer line on the other show how the sculptor made a fixed figure appear to pitch into motion.

This cast records a different casualty from the same Aphaia battle scene, figure III of the east pediment. SMK acquired it in 1898, and the historical cast may contain earlier restorations. Examining this casualty beside the other Aphaia casts shows how a shared narrative could accommodate different kinds of collapse and resistance. The raised sword arm projects above the reclining torso. Its arc lets the figure register both exertion and collapse within the shallow, horizontal space of the pediment.

This plaster follows east-pediment figure IV from the Temple of Aphaia, dated about 485–480 BCE. It entered SMK’s collection in 1898. The running pose can be understood in relation to the pediment’s shallow field, where momentum had to remain readable from below. Both arms reach ahead as the rear foot trails. The body reads as a forward diagonal from ankle to shoulder, with the bent front knee taking the implied weight.

This plaster reproduces figure XI of the east pediment at the Temple of Aphaia on Aegina. The Greek prototype dates to about 485–480 BCE, and SMK acquired the cast in 1898. The pediment originally determined how the warrior could fit within a diminishing architectural space, a constraint the plaster helps make visible. The round shield anchors one end of the wounded body. From the opposite end, an extended leg and a bent knee create different slopes suited to the taper of a pediment.

This plaster concept model by an unrecorded maker refers to Marc Quinn's portrait of Alison Lapper. A monumental version of the portrait appeared at the London 2012 Paralympics. A plaster concept model has a different function from the monumental public portrait and records the circulation of its design at another scale. The head and upper body rise directly from the seated pose. The rounded abdomen anchors the composition and makes Lapper's pregnancy central to the portrait.

SMK acquired this plaster cast in 1898. It follows a Renaissance marble associated with the Villa del Poggio Imperiale in Florence, formerly attributed to Michelangelo. The cast preserves a Renaissance reading of antique loss and repose, while the former attribution remains part of the history of its study. Adonis’s reclining body makes a long line along the base. The bent leg lifts the eye briefly before it returns to the dog and the figure’s low, resting silhouette.

This reduced plaster transmits the design of a monumental Quirinal Dioscurus. SMK relates it to a plaster model dated 1799 at Thorvaldsens Museum, with the precise chain of copies still uncertain. Reduction changes the conditions of viewing a giant whose design was intended for an urban space and an audience standing far below it. The muscular body and mantle read against the compact mass of the armor-shaped support. Reduction makes the paired verticals easy to compare in a single glance.

SMK acquired this plaster cast in 1899. Its Roman marble prototype, probably the restored sculpture in Berlin, follows a fourth-century BCE Greek type. A restored antique prototype makes this cast evidence of both classical iconography and later decisions about what a complete statue should look like. The raised arm opens the torso on one side while the weight shifts toward the draped support. SMK records the penis as absent in the surviving form.

SMK acquired this cast after a Roman marble in 1902. The ancient torso once stood in the Palazzo Valentini, and an attached head has been associated with Diomedes, though the figure's identity remains uncertain. The plaster preserves a fragment as an object of study, letting later viewers inspect an antique torso without inventing its missing pose. The fragment concentrates attention on the continuous modeling of the chest, abdomen and hips. Turn the model to see how the torso widens and narrows through the upper thighs.

This bronze faun was found at Pompeii. The city’s burial in 79 CE supplies the latest possible date for the ancient figure. Its archaeological date is bounded by the destruction of Pompeii, making it a comparatively secure point in the history of the dancing faun type. One raised arm extends the line of the chest, while the legs take unequal steps. Rotate the bronze to catch the twist through the waist and the open spaces around the limbs.

This Roman marble probably belonged to a version of the Greek sculptural group known as The Invitation to Dance. Only the faun’s torso survives. A fragment can preserve the ancient sculptor’s solution to turning the torso even when the limbs that completed the movement are gone. Compare the direction of the shoulders with that of the hips. The two axes meet in a spiral, carrying a sense of dance through the fragment.

This Roman marble follows a satyr type associated with Praxiteles. The scan identifies the version formerly in the Palazzo Ruspoli and acquired for Munich in 1812. The leaning body is close to a classical formula in which a support provides both a practical brace and a reason for relaxed posture. The tree carries part of the figure’s weight, letting the hip drift outward and the torso ease to one side. Compare the rough detail of the support with the more continuous contours of the body.

This Roman marble in Leiden pairs Bacchus with a satyr and panther, figures associated with wine and revelry. Their physical closeness also supports a reading of same-sex intimacy. Bacchus’s company gives the sculptor a vocabulary of animal movement and human instability against which the god’s body can be read. Bacchus gives part of his weight to the satyr. Compare the lean of the supported figure with the stance of his companion and the low mass of the panther.

This second-century Roman marble takes its name from the painter Peter Lely, a former owner. It is now at the British Museum on loan from the Royal Collection. The work’s later collection name records a chapter of its modern reception distinct from the antique bath image it preserves. The low crouch folds the torso while the head turns sharply over one shoulder. The twist makes an apparently private moment open outward to the viewer.

This fragment of a Roman Silenus is displayed at Narbo Via in Narbonne. The scan publisher proposes a late first- to second-century CE date. Silenus provides a counterpoint to idealized images of youthful gods through his place in the antique repertory of older, heavier bodies. The beard and textured body hair sit against the rounder planes of the belly. The inclined head follows the lean through the ribs and gives the fragment much of its character.

The Louvre sculpture combines an ancient Roman marble of Hermaphroditus with a mattress carved by Gian Lorenzo Bernini in 1620. The Roman figure is part of a classical tradition of using a change in viewpoint to alter what a body seems to be. Bernini’s mattress gives that slow discovery an additional test of perception. Its seams and compressed folds appear soft despite the stone, even as the torso and crossed legs keep the body turned partly away.

In this second-century Roman marble, Dionysus is accompanied by the bearded Pan and a panther. Their closeness belongs to a mythological group centered on the god and his companions. The grouping can be read through the association between the wine god, Pan and the animal, which gives each figure an iconographic role. Compare the height of the two gods and the short interval between their bodies. The panther draws attention to the ground beneath a pair otherwise held together at shoulder and arm level.

This second-century Roman marble after a type associated with Lysippos was restored in the eighteenth century by Bartolomeo Cavaceppi. It is now at the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek. The restoration belongs to the sculpture’s eighteenth-century reception and should be distinguished from the history of the Roman marble. Hermes turns his head away from the foot he is tending. The lifted leg and angled torso let the viewer see both the ordinary action and the full extent of the turn.

This marble group of Pan and Bacchus dates to the first or second century CE and is held by the Musée de la Romanité. The model shows the surviving object before digital restoration. The pairing gives two distinct mythological figures a shared sculptural space, where position and scale can do interpretive work. The long curve of the seated body remains legible where heads and limbs are interrupted. Rotate the group to compare the compact seat and base with the surviving figure’s reclining line.

This small Roman marble dates to the later second century CE and retains traces of paint. It shows Aphrodite taking off a sandal before bathing. Surviving color matters to the history of this marble because it complicates the later association of antique sculpture with unpainted white stone. The lifted foot forces the whole body to rebalance. Turn the figure to see how the standing leg, turned torso, and reaching hand work together.

This Netherlandish alabaster of around 1600 shows Hercules lifting Antaeus clear of the earth, his source of strength. Renaissance statuettes of the subject have also been read in the history of same-sex desire. The small alabaster group belongs to a tradition of making an outsized myth legible at close scale through a self-contained tangle of limbs. The lower body braces as the lifted figure curls and twists. The same contacts that make the hold believable give the struggle a close, almost joint silhouette.

Bernini carved the marble for Cardinal Scipione Borghese in 1622–1625. Apollo reaches toward Daphne as her fingers become leaves and bark overtakes her body. The branching outline makes the transformation legible as the viewer walks around the group.

François Barois carved this marble at the Académie de France in Rome in the 1680s, copying the celebrated Farnese Venus. Such copies carried admired ancient compositions into French academic practice and collecting. Venus lifts her drapery and turns to look back, creating a route for the viewer from the raised hand down through the folds and around to the exposed body. The arrangement makes the act of looking part of the sculpture’s subject.

Allegrain made this marble in 1767. The Louvre identifies the scene as Venus leaving her bath. The eighteenth-century bath subject gives a goddess an ordinary action, a way of bringing bodily movement into an elevated genre. Turn the model to follow the torso's change of direction and the folds of the cloth. Both draw the eye around what first appears to be a simple standing pose.

Canova modeled this water nymph in 1815–1817 and carved the marble in 1820–1823. The original is at the National Gallery of Art in Washington. The contrast between the nymph and her support allows Canova to set highly finished flesh against a more materially descriptive surface. The figure turns her head back across the sweep of her body. Follow where the long line of the pose meets the folds of the animal skin beneath her.

Auguste Carbonneaux cast Bosio’s bronze in 1824. The work shows Hercules fighting Achelous, who has become a serpent in their rivalry for Deianira. The serpent gives Bosio a continuous counterline against which the muscular figure and its athletic effort can be read. The braced legs and raised torso carry the hero’s force. Turn the group to follow the serpent’s coils as they run across that line and draw the struggle sideways.

Étienne-Jules Ramey’s 1826 marble stages the fight between Theseus and the Minotaur. It is now in the Louvre. The myth offered academic sculptors a reason to bind contrasting bodies into a single composition that responds to changes of viewpoint. The figures hold one another through a chain of grips, bent joints, and opposing weight. Walk around the group to see where one body supports or checks the other.

Clésinger made this marble of a follower of Bacchus in 1848, a year after his separate Woman Bitten by a Snake. The work is now in the Petit Palais. The bacchante belongs to a nineteenth-century use of antiquity that brought palpable flesh into subjects sanctioned by myth. The twist interrupts the long line of the reclining figure. Rotate the model to see how the movement travels through the torso.

Carpeaux’s plaster group of about 1872 is related to The Dance for the Paris Opéra. The larger work became controversial for the naturalism of its dancers. A canonical three-figure subject offers an occasion to vary closely related poses rather than simply repeating an emblem. Joined hands carry the eye upward, while bent knees and turns at the waist send it around the base. Seen from another side, a different dancer takes the lead.

Frederic Leighton made this life-size bronze in 1877. Tate holds the work, which brings a study of muscular balance to a struggle with a python. Leighton’s group makes an academic life study work as a sculpture in the round by using the snake to connect different views. Follow the snake around the leg, then look up the back of the figure. The rear thigh and buttock bear much of the tension as the torso turns away.

Rodin modeled this figure in 1880–1882 and enlarged it in the early twentieth century. The scan shows the Hirshhorn’s bronze, cast in 1962. Rodin’s decision to enlarge an intensely folded figure makes the squat a monumental composition and exposes a back usually subordinated to the face. Look from the side and back to see how the deep squat brings the legs close to the torso. The raised hips become the highest and most conspicuous mass.

Jean-François Etcheto carved this life-size marble Bacchante in 1889. Her identity as a follower of Bacchus gave a late nineteenth-century sculptor a mythological setting for the figure. The bacchante’s mythological role permits a study of bodily motion that a more formal civic figure would have difficulty sustaining. One elbow opens away from the waist, where the hands gather across the body. The line of the free hip continues down the leg in a gentle curve.

This 1889 terracotta is held by Nationalmuseum in Stockholm. The mythological title evokes the Danaids, whose punishment was to fill a vessel that could never hold water. The story’s endless labor is suggested through a single exhausted body, one of the ways Rodin concentrated a larger narrative into a pose. The folded body makes a broad arc over the support. Turn to the rear to see how the bent legs and lowered upper body pull the pose inward.

Rodin modeled this figure in the early 1880s, and the National Gallery of Art’s marble was carved in 1909. The work is known as The Sphinx. The name brings a mythic and psychological charge to a figure whose effect is carried by its compressed pose. The kneeling woman presses forward onto her hands and raises her head. Contrast the smooth torso with the rough marble where the base meets the figure.

Eduard Hauser’s Leda and the Swan forms the upper group of the Nymph Fountain. Made in the early twentieth century, the fountain moved to its current Klosterneuburg setting in 1956. The fountain’s architecture shapes the sculpture’s first sightline, establishing a viewing angle that the digital model lets you undo. Look at how the encounter rises from the lower supporting figures. The upward movement makes the woman and bird legible as the fountain’s central group.

This bronze stands left of the former ministry entrance at Radetzkystraße 2 in Vienna. The scan publisher places its composition between 1915 and 1922 within Hanak's series of outdoor figures. Public placement makes the silhouette important because a passerby may recognize the kneeling gesture before seeing any surface detail. The knees form a low base from which the upper body rises. The hand lifted toward the head draws the eye up along the torso.

The scan publisher identifies this outdoor bronze on Vienna's Vordere Zollamtsstraße as a work by Anton Hanak dated 1922. The date of this cast remains unconfirmed. Viewed beside Hanak’s other Vienna figures, this reclining type contributes a horizontal counterpart to bodies organized by standing and kneeling. The arms lift to support the head, interrupting the low line of the reclining pose. From the side, the lifted elbows make a distinct shape against the space above the body.

Georges-Clément de Swiecinski carved this group from local Sarrailh stone in 1938, drawing inspiration from the poetry of Francis Jammes. It stands at the Musée de Guéthary. The literary inspiration and local quarry connect a classical vocabulary of bodies with a particular regional setting. The two women lean together around a shared center. Follow where each figure’s weight falls as the outline shifts from a close embrace to two distinct bodies.

Georg Kolbe designed this pairing of the gods of war and love in 1940. The bronze in Berlin’s Georg-Kolbe-Hain was cast in 1963. The separation between design and casting is part of this bronze’s history, a distinction that often matters for twentieth-century public sculpture. Their feet plant the figures side by side, but their heads send attention in different directions. Follow the gap between the bodies as it opens and closes with your viewpoint.

Stijović’s Nude was recorded in Belgrade’s Manjež Park. The scan documentation dates the work to 1957. The location establishes how a modern standing nude came to be encountered as a public body in a park. The rounded hips and back carry much of the silhouette. From this angle, the upper limbs create a compact turn over the fuller mass below.

Augustin's life-size bronze stands at the Stephansplatz entrance to Hamburg's Planten un Blomen. Municipal records give both 1976 and 1977 for the work. Its appearance in Stephansplatz brings a familiar sculptural type into direct contact with the changing scale of a city square. The raised knee and braced arm give the reclining figure a broad, angular outline. The straight edges of the support make these changes of direction more pronounced.

The Royal Museum workshop in Munich reconstructed this Discobolus in plaster from prototypes in two Roman museums. It entered SMK’s collection in 1902. The reconstruction records a modern attempt to synthesize several ancient witnesses and is itself part of the afterlife of Myron’s design. The discus arm describes a wide arc over a closely folded body. The bent knees and turning waist compress the pose, making the next instant of movement feel imminent.

The scan publisher attributes the work to Félix-Maurice Charpentier and identifies the material as marble. The precise object, date and holding collection remain unconfirmed. The reclining format can be considered within the tradition of the sculpted nude while the precise identity of this scanned example remains open. Follow the twist of the torso across the support. A side view makes the shift between the body's axis and its resting surface easier to see.

The bronze at the Ringling is attributed to the Chiurazzi Foundry and follows the antique Sleeping Satyr type. Its casting date remains unknown. The cast gives the sleeping type another material life, showing why a museum’s bronze and an antique marble should be dated separately. An arm arcs over the head while the legs settle at different angles. From the side, follow how much of the figure’s weight appears to sink into the rocky seat.

This marble of Pan belongs to the Heraklion Archaeological Museum. The available scan documentation identifies the subject but gives no date or maker. The lack of a secure date limits stylistic attribution, even as the subject can be understood within antique images of Pan. Look at the slight turn around the narrow waist and the difference in height between the shoulders. The broken edges keep the surviving torso in focus, even when viewed from the side.

The Uffizi marble is a Roman Imperial version of a Hellenistic subject that survives in several ancient examples, including one in the Louvre. The Florentine example records another transmission of the antique sleeping type, useful to compare with the version on Bernini’s mattress. Look at the figure from both sides to see different aspects of its combined anatomy. The low pose and turned body make the walk around the sculpture part of reading it.
