This Roman marble from the first century BCE follows a Greek type associated with Timotheos. It depicts Leda holding Zeus in the form of a swan. In this Roman version the bird is indispensable to recognizing the myth, even where it can be mistaken for part of the drapery. Look at the narrow space between the swan, Leda’s thigh, and the cloth. That point of contact gives the myth its physical focus.

Clodion modeled this late eighteenth-century terracotta group, now at the Memorial Art Gallery in Rochester. Its companions belong to the mythological world of Bacchus. Terracotta modeling suited the small mythological groups through which Clodion put movement, humor and intimacy in close dialogue. The lifted arms and turning torsos make the group expand above its ornate base. Move to a lower viewpoint to see how the reclining figures sit against the drapery.

Johan Tobias Sergel began this Carrara marble in Rome in 1775 and completed it in Stockholm in 1804. Mars supports the wounded Venus in a scene from the Iliad. The group is an example of how Neoclassical artists could use antique myth to make a vulnerable or injured body central. Follow how Venus’s weight leans into Mars. A turn around the group shows the supporting arm and the changing gaps between their torsos.

Augustin Courtet exhibited a model of this encounter in 1849. The bronze in Lyon’s Parc de la Tête d’Or followed in 1850–1852. Courtet gives the hybrid creatures a convincing physical relationship, a nineteenth-century exercise in making a mythic encounter feel bodily immediate. The centauress gathers the faun toward her, pulling the two profiles into one space. Move to the side to see how the animal body carries the weight of the encounter.

Jean-Baptiste Auguste Clésinger carved this mythological pair in marble in 1869. The work is now at the Minneapolis Institute of Art. The bacchic subject gave nineteenth-century sculptors a mythological setting for bodily contact, unstable poses and the push and pull of competing figures. From behind, the bacchante’s turn carries the eye across her back and hip. Continue around and the satyr comes into view as the counterweight to her extended body.

Rodin first modeled Paolo and Francesca, the doomed lovers in Dante’s Inferno, for The Gates of Hell. Making them an independent sculpture loosened the embrace from its place in the larger narrative. In the marble, the pair joins at the lips and through the encircling arms, while the turning torsos and offset knees keep the two bodies distinct. The rear view makes the uneven distribution of weight especially clear.

Rodin developed this group in connection with The Gates of Hell before 1887. The scanned Cantor Foundation bronze was shown in Portland in 2017, and its cast date is unrecorded. The larger project supplied Rodin with figures and gestures he could reuse, reposition and cast as self-contained groups. Compare the directions of the entwined bodies. The long outlines are still legible in the untextured scan, even where surface detail is limited.

This third version of Claudel's waltzing couple belongs to an edition of 25 published by Eugène Blot. The date of this cast is unconfirmed. The edition history is significant because the cast’s drapery and formal balance belong to this particular version of a revised composition. Trace the forward tilt of the dancers' bodies and then the sweep of the drapery. The bronze translates the turn of the dance into a continuous curve.

Rodin modeled Iris in 1891, adapting a dancer’s pose to the mythological messenger. This bronze was lent by Iris Cantor to the Portland Art Museum’s 2017 Rodin exhibition. The messenger’s gesture gives a classical name to one of Rodin’s independent experiments with what a fragmentary body can express. The extended leg and arched body make a forceful diagonal. The deliberate gaps at head and arm leave the remaining limbs to suggest an instant of flight.

This 1893 marble entered Harvard’s Fogg Museum through Grenville L. Winthrop’s bequest. The kneeling lover and upright seated woman give their encounter an uneven balance. The title leaves room for an allegory of devotion, while the differing heights of the figures make reverence physically legible. Follow the man’s forward incline up to the woman’s torso. Their smooth bodies rise from a roughly worked base that makes their small gestures stand out.

The Société Nouvelle des Bronzes cast Jef Lambeaux’s group in Brussels in 1901. The large bronze is displayed outdoors in the park at Mariemont. An allegorical title and demonstrative grouping place the work within the history of public sculpture as an argument made through bodies. Follow the forward bend of the upper figure and the mass of forms packed beneath it. Seen in silhouette, those low, compressed forms make the rise of the group feel unstable and active.

Signed and dated 1903, this bronze caused controversy at the 1905 Liège exhibition. It later found a permanent setting in the city’s Parc de la Boverie. The woman’s counterattack reverses the conventions of a pursuit scene, so the group’s narrative depends on who has the leverage at each angle. The woman turns to bite the ear of the faun who has attacked her. Watch the shift from the tangle of limbs to that small point of contact, where the direction of force reverses.

Vigeland made this bronze in 1905 and returned to related embraces in several distinct compositions. The scan records the work outside Oslo’s former National Gallery. Vigeland’s related groups make the embrace a recurring problem of sculptural balance, with each version finding a different distribution of weight. The seated man curves his arms around the woman stretched across his lap. Follow the turn of his back and shoulders to their meeting foreheads.

Rodin assembled these figures from earlier studies in 1906–07. The title The Birth of Venus, also known as The Aurore, invites a reading of the group as an emergence. The alternative titles show how Rodin’s figures could suggest a subject through movement and association, with the title influencing how the rise is read. Look where a polished limb meets roughly worked stone. Turn the group to see the two bodies at different heights and the changing extent to which each appears to have broken free of the block.

Lorieux carved this marble in 1907. Also called The Kiss, it stands in the Parc Jean-Rameau in Mont-de-Marsan. The competing titles shift the group between a named kiss and a seasonal metaphor, drawing attention to the role of titles in reception. Both figures incline toward the point where their faces meet. The kiss brings two separate bodies into a single arch.

Eric Gill carved this Hoptonwood stone relief in 1910–1911. Tate identifies sex and embracing among the work’s subjects. Gill’s shallow relief makes the relationship of the two bodies a problem of contour and overlap within the limits of a stone surface. Trace how the two figures fit inside the vertical edges of the block. Overlapping contours give the embrace depth while the slab holds it flat.

Kai Nielsen’s 1918 sandstone group shows Leda with Zeus disguised as a swan. The original is in Statens Museum for Kunst in Copenhagen. Nielsen’s compact version gives the myth the density of a carved block, with little room for the expansive gestures of many earlier Ledas. Follow the broad surfaces where the woman and bird press together. Their contact makes a dense central mass that holds even as the outline changes around it.

Ernesto Canto da Maya made this terracotta group in 1934. The Museu Nacional Soares dos Reis places it within his exploration of erotic feeling. The modeled terracotta lets pressure and contact accumulate in a single mass, making the group read differently from Rodin’s more expansive treatment of the kiss. The joined arms have an echo in the two pairs of bent legs below. The roundness and smooth surface of the bodies help the embrace read as one continuous volume.

Jane Aypel’s 1993 stone group was given to Versailles in 1995, according to its plaque. It stands near the Hôtel de Ville. The title asks the viewer to read relations between the two bodies, making contact and shared balance more important than isolated anatomy. The overlap of the two bodies makes the embrace legible before the faces. Compare the smooth shared outline with the roughness of the seat beneath it.

This 2007 granite sculpture accompanies A Moment Before the Kiss in Tallinn’s Musumägi park. The pair contrasts standing anticipation with a kneeling embrace. Placed with its companion, the work asks how far intimacy can be read from weight, contact and distance between figures. Follow the curve from the broad base through the folded legs and into the joined shoulders. Compare the compact outline here with the taller silhouette of its companion.

Tauno Kangro made this granite pair in 2007 for Tallinn’s Musumägi park, where it stands with A Moment After the Kiss. The paired monuments turn a fleeting gesture into a before-and-after sequence that visitors can reconstruct by moving through the park. The bodies touch almost from top to bottom, while a narrow gap remains between the faces. That small interval makes the suspended moment readable in a heavy material.

The scan publisher credits the Guatemalan sculptor Luis Carlos. His full name, the date, and the sculpture’s collection are unrecorded. A public attribution based on the scan should remain provisional until an inscription or civic record identifies the exact object. The two nudes form a nearly continuous vertical outline. Turn the work until the narrow gaps between bodies make the embrace easier to trace.

Nordhausen identifies Johann Ludwig Miel as the sculptor and records the restored group’s return to Bahnhofstraße. Its creation date remains unknown. The fountain setting makes this telling of Leda a work to encounter in passing and from below, as well as an image of a myth. Examine where the bird’s shape meets Leda’s torso. Seen from the side, the encounter is held in a small area of overlap between the two bodies.

This public sculpture stands in Saint-Gilles, Brussels. The scan publisher attributes it to Jean-Marie Abel, though the attribution and date remain unverified. In a civic setting, an embrace is visible from ordinary street approaches, which can change how its apparent privacy is experienced. Look upward from the narrow support to the point where the figures meet. The rising shape makes the kiss the point at which the whole composition comes together.

The Brooklyn Museum dates this small limestone relief to Ptolemaic Egypt. The surviving slab records an image of intercourse, and its present scale and depth are firmer evidence than any inference about its original use. Look for the points where overlapping limbs separate into two people. A few carved changes in level give the intertwined bodies legibility and make their contact register within a shallow field.

This first-century Roman oil lamp belongs to the Museu de Badalona, which identifies its subject as a kneeling woman performing oral sex on a lyre-playing satyr. The lamp turns the equipment of everyday lighting into a setting for mythological comedy and a sexual scene. The scene fits within the lamp’s circular upper surface. Look at how the bent limbs fill the curve and how the relief sits within the practical shape of the vessel.
